proof_text:
Suppose for contradiction that $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is nonempty
yet possesses no least element. Let $P(n)$ be the assertion that
$n \notin A$. We prove that $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ by
strong induction. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and assume that $P(k)$ holds
for all $k < n$, meaning no natural number strictly smaller than $n$
belongs to $A$. If $n$ were in $A$, then because no strictly smaller
natural number belongs to $A$, $n$ would be the least element of $A$,
contradicting our hypothesis that $A$ has no least element. Therefore
$n \notin A$, which establishes $P(n)$. By strong induction,
$n \notin A$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, which forces
$A = \emptyset$. This contradicts the assumption that $A$ is nonempty.

Theorem:
given: A \:(nonempty)::subset:/ \naturals
then:
. exists: m is \natural
  suchThat:
  . m "in"? A
  . forAll: n is \natural
    where: n "in"? A
    then: m \:natural.leq?:/ n
